findings.title: Old local recovery codes stay valid when new codes are stored in user storage
findings.body:
Before this change, `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential` always ran, and it deletes the user's existing stored recovery-codes credential before creating the new one. Now, when `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` returns true (the codes went to user storage), the local provider is skipped, so any previously stored local recovery-codes credential is never deleted.

`UserCredentialManager.isValid` checks the user-storage validator first and then falls through to the local `CredentialInputValidator`s. So a code the user entered that fails in user storage is then checked against the stale local codes and is accepted.

Result: after a user regenerates recovery codes (for example after an upgrade where the provider starts accepting this type, or after a provider config change), the old codes that were supposed to be replaced can still be used to log in. The user-storage branch should also remove any existing local recovery-codes credential.

findings.title: All-codes-used cleanup targets the local store even when the credential came from user storage
findings.body:
`optUserCredentialFound` now comes from `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`, which prefers credentials returned by the user storage provider (`getFederatedCredentialsStream`). When `allCodesUsed()` is true, the code still calls `credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(id)`. That only touches Keycloak's local/federated JPA credential store, never the user storage provider.

For a provider-supplied credential this has two failure modes:
- If the id belongs to the provider, the call is a silent no-op. The exhausted credential stays, and `isConfiguredFor` keeps returning true.
- If the provider returns a model without an id, the call receives null. `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues` leaves the id unset, and the test provider's `getCredentials` does exactly this. With a null id, `em.find(..., null)` in the JPA store throws `IllegalArgumentException`, so the login fails with a 500.

For federated credentials the code should take a different path, such as `disableCredentialType(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE)` or no removal at all.

findings.title: Test provider accepts any of the codes and never consumes them, so single-use is untested
findings.body:
`isValid` for recovery codes returns true if the input matches any stored code. It never marks the code as used and does not check that it is the code the login form asked for (`getNextRecoveryAuthnCode`).

The new `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` therefore only checks that some valid code is accepted once. It would still pass if:
- the wrong code number were entered,
- a code could be reused,
- the next login asked for the same code again.

The core recovery-code contract (single-use, sequential) is not exercised at all for the user-storage path.

findings.title: Changing the "4.8.3-compatible" provider alters what existing OTP backward-compat tests cover
findings.body:
The class Javadoc says this provider mimics a Keycloak 4.8.3 implementation and should not need changes for newer versions. This PR adds the newer `getCredentials` API and gives OTP credentials a generated id (`newOTP.setId(...)`).

As a result, the existing OTP tests no longer run against an old-style provider. For example, `testOTPSetupAndRemoveThroughAccountMgmtAndLogin` (issue 19575) used to get the placeholder `otp-id` from the account REST endpoint (`CredentialHelper.createUserStorageCredentialRepresentation`). It will now receive the real OTP credential with a UUID from `getFederatedCredentialsStream`.

The legacy placeholder path that these tests were written to protect loses coverage. The recovery-code support would be better placed in a separate, modern test provider.
